_comment: Pre-market brief. Regenerated on a schedule and committed; the site only renders it. See tools/market-brief.md for how it is produced and what each field must contain. Everything here is written in our own words from sourced reporting — do not paste licensed article text into this file.
headline: Core CPI ran hot into an FOMC that is now 90% priced to hike
standfirst: Stocks closed the week higher anyway, the 10-year is at 4.96% — the highest since 2023 — and Wednesday brings a decision, a dot plot and a press conference. The BoE follows Thursday, the BoJ Friday.

bullets.title: The inflation data did not cooperate, and the market bought it anyway
bullets.text: August CPI held at 3.4% year-over-year as expected, but core rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected — a four-month high. PPI the day before came in at 5.4% year-over-year versus 5.3% expected, with July revised up. The S&P still added 0.86% Friday to close at 7,656.98, the Dow 0.98% and the Nasdaq 0.96%, and the VIX fell 11% to 15.84. Equities are trading the fact that the hike is now known, not the inflation that caused it.

bullets.title: The hike is priced at nine-in-ten, and the curve has already moved
bullets.text: Futures odds went from roughly 61% before PPI to 72% after it and 86–91% after CPI — a step to 3.75–4.00%. Meanwhile the 10-year finished at 4.96% after touching 4.97%, its highest since late 2023, the 30-year at 5.35% and the 2-year at 4.63%, leaving 2s10s at 33bp and 3m10y at 89bp. The long end moved more than the front, which is the market saying it believes the inflation more than it believes any one meeting. When a move is priced this far in advance, the tradeable content sits in the projections and the press conference, not in the 14:00 ET statement.

bullets.title: Oil gave back the geopolitical premium
bullets.text: WTI topped $100 midweek and then fell 2.37% Friday to $100.05 on reports easing Strait of Hormuz fears; Brent sat at $104.61. Energy was the channel that pushed this inflation scare in the first place, so an oil tape that stops going up removes the most direct route to another upside surprise — and removes it right before the meeting.

bullets.title: The ECB has already gone, and two more central banks follow this week
bullets.text: The ECB hiked 25bp on 10 September, taking the deposit rate to 2.50% effective the 16th, with staff forecasting 3.0% inflation this year falling to 2.1% by 2028. Markets price roughly 79% odds of another move on 29 October. The Bank of England decides Thursday (a hold at 3.75% is expected) and the Bank of Japan Friday, where a move to 1.25% is the base case. Three decisions in three days is a week that does not let currency positions sit.

bullets.title: The dollar is the thing that has not confirmed
bullets.text: DXY finished around 99.11 and gold at $4,408.90 despite a full week of hawkish repricing. If rates were the whole story the dollar would be higher and gold lower. Either the dollar catches up this week or the rate move is closer to done than the headlines suggest — that divergence is the cleanest single tell on the board right now.

calendar.event: China industrial production and retail sales
calendar.note: Nothing major from the US. A quiet Monday before a loaded week usually means range, not trend.

calendar.event: German and Eurozone ZEW, US Empire State manufacturing
calendar.note: FOMC begins behind closed doors. Nothing here is big enough to break structure — the last such session of the week.

calendar.event: US retail sales and import/export prices (August)
calendar.note: The last hard consumer read the committee sees before it votes, and it prints five and a half hours ahead of them. Import prices land in the same minute and matter more than usual with the tariff channel live.
18:00 UTC. The dots are the event, not the hike. Press conference 14:30 ET.
11:00 UTC. Hold at 3.75% expected — the vote split is where the GBP move comes from.

calendar.event: US jobless claims, Philadelphia Fed, housing starts, building permits
calendar.note: Four releases into one print time, the morning after an FOMC. Thin book, wide quotes.
A move to 1.25% from 1.00% is the base case. Watch the yen, then watch what the yen does to Japanese equities in dollars.
Followed by Conference Board leading indicators. A quiet close to a loud week.

sessionNote: Monday and Tuesday are the only two sessions this week with no scheduled US event large enough to break structure. If you need clean conditions to take a setup, they are at the front of the week, not the back. From Wednesday 14:00 ET onward you are trading inside a three-day central bank window across three currencies, and the overnight gaps that come out of a BoJ decision are not the kind you manage with a stop sitting at yesterday's low.
watchOut: The trap this week is the FOMC itself being a non-event. A hike priced at nine-in-ten does not move price when it lands — the move comes from the dots and the press conference half an hour later, and it frequently comes in the opposite direction to the first reaction. If your rule is to stand aside for scheduled releases, extend it through 15:00 ET Wednesday rather than stopping at the statement.

archive.headline: Core CPI at a four-month high, hike odds jump to ~90%
archive.summary: Headline CPI held at 3.4% year-over-year but core rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected. Energy added 2.1% and gasoline 3.9%; airline fares rose 2.7%. Equities rallied regardless — S&P +0.86%, VIX −11% — while the 10-year touched 4.97%.

archive.headline: PPI beats, ECB hikes to 2.50%
archive.summary: August PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year against 5.3% expected with July revised up from flat. The ECB raised its deposit rate 25bp to 2.50% effective 16 September and cut its 2028 inflation forecast to 2.1%. September hike odds moved from 61% to 72%.

archive.headline: Oil tops $100, Dow sheds 400 more
archive.summary: Brent broke $100 for the first time since July and the 10-year yield hit a three-year high. Amgen fell over 10% on a failed cardiovascular trial and software names sold off. Barclays nonetheless lifted its year-end S&P target to 7,950.
